subject: PHS
vignette: An 82-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease is scheduled for elective cataract surgery. During the preoperative visit she accurately describes the procedure, explains that clouding of her lens is why the surgeon recommends it, weighs the risks against her difficulty driving, and states clearly that she wants the surgery. On the morning of surgery she is found to be acutely confused from a urinary tract infection, and her son asks that her consent be cancelled since she "no longer knows what she agreed to."
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: Cancel the surgery, because her current confusion makes the consent she gave invalid and a new consent is required.
Proceed with the surgery as planned, because decisions made with capacity cannot be revoked simply because the patient later loses capacity.
Proceed with the surgery, but first obtain written consent from the son, who can now authorize care on her behalf.
Obtain a judicial determination of incompetence before proceeding, since dementia prevents valid consent.
Delay the surgery until the confusion resolves, then have her sign a new consent form even if she repeats the same decision.

explanation_correct: Decision-making capacity is assessed at the time of a specific healthcare decision. At her preoperative visit, the patient demonstrated all four components — understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a choice — so her consent was validly given. Decisions made with capacity cannot be revoked simply because the patient later loses capacity. Her current delirium does not retroactively invalidate the earlier decision.

explanation_incorrect.A: Treating the consent as invalid disregards the rule that a decision made while capacitated stands even if the patient later loses capacity.
explanation_incorrect.C: Surrogate consent is not needed because a valid consent already exists; the son cannot retroactively re-authorize a decision the patient already made with capacity.
explanation_incorrect.D: Judicial determination of competence is unnecessary; her mild dementia did not impair capacity at the time of consent, and a court order is not required.
explanation_incorrect.E: Requiring a new consent assumes the prior one was invalid; in fact, a capacitated decision remains binding even after subsequent loss of capacity.

educationalObjective: Decisions made with decision-making capacity cannot be revoked simply because the patient later loses capacity.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 28-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia, well controlled on an antipsychotic medication and without any current psychotic symptoms, is evaluated for new severe headache. The physician recommends a lumbar puncture, but the patient declines, saying he does not want the procedure at this time. A medical student asks whether his psychiatric diagnosis means his refusal can be ignored.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's decision-making capacity?

options.text: He retains capacity to refuse the lumbar puncture, because intellectual disabilities and mental illnesses are not exclusion criteria unless the condition presently impairs his ability to make healthcare decisions.
He lacks capacity to refuse the lumbar puncture, because a diagnosis of schizophrenia is itself sufficient to declare a patient unable to make medical decisions.
He lacks capacity to refuse the lumbar puncture, because only patients without any psychiatric history can give or withhold consent for invasive procedures.
His capacity is irrelevant, because a judge must first determine his competency before any treatment decision can be made.
His capacity can be presumed only for low-risk decisions, and any refusal of an invasive procedure requires a court order to be valid.

explanation_correct: Decision-making capacity is assessed functionally for a specific decision at a specific time. Intellectual disabilities and mental illnesses are not exclusion criteria unless the patient's condition presently impairs their ability to make healthcare decisions. This patient is currently asymptomatic and has no acute psychotic symptoms impairing his reasoning, so he retains capacity to refuse the procedure. The diagnosis alone never removes capacity.

explanation_incorrect.B: A diagnosis of schizophrenia does not by itself remove capacity; only present impairment of the patient's ability to make the specific decision matters.
explanation_incorrect.C: There is no requirement of an unblemished psychiatric history; a stable, currently asymptomatic patient with mental illness retains full decision-making capacity.
explanation_incorrect.D: Capacity for a specific healthcare decision is determined by the physician; judicial determination of competency is a separate, more global legal process.
explanation_incorrect.E: Capacity is not risk-stratified by courts; the physician assesses the patient's ability to make the particular decision, however invasive it may be.

educationalObjective: Mental illness and intellectual disability do not preclude decision-making capacity unless the condition presently impairs the specific decision.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with early dementia is being assessed before consenting to a colonoscopy. She accurately describes the procedure as "a camera that looks inside my large intestine." She states that she wants to go ahead with it. However, when the physician asks what her condition means to her and why she thinks the doctor is recommending this course of treatment, she is unable to connect the recommendation to her rectal bleeding and says, "I don't really know why you want to do it."
question: Which of the four major components of decision-making is most impaired in this patient?

options.text: Understanding
Expressing a choice
Reasoning
Appreciation
Voluntariness

explanation_correct: Appreciation is the component in which the patient articulates what the condition means to them and why the doctor is recommending the proposed course of treatment. This patient cannot connect the recommendation to her own situation (rectal bleeding), so appreciation is impaired. Understanding is intact because she can accurately describe the procedure, and expressing a choice is intact because she has stated a clear preference. The four components — understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a choice — are each assessed separately.

explanation_incorrect.A: Understanding is intact: she correctly describes what the procedure involves, which is the knowledge component of capacity.
explanation_incorrect.B: Expressing a choice is intact: she has clearly stated that she wants to proceed with the colonoscopy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Reasoning — how she weighs her options — is not the component tested by her failure to explain why the treatment is being recommended.
explanation_incorrect.E: Voluntariness is a requirement of informed consent (freedom from coercion), not one of the four components of decision-making capacity, and no coercion is described.

educationalObjective: Appreciation — the ability to explain what the condition means to the patient and why treatment is recommended — is one of the four components of decision-making capacity.

subject: PHS
vignette: During rounds, an intern proposes, "Mrs. Ortiz is clearly psychotic, so she is incompetent and we should ask a judge to declare it so we can treat her without her consent." The patient in question has acute agitation but has never been formally evaluated for her ability to make the specific decision at hand.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate correction of the intern's statement by the attending physician?

options.text: "You are right that she is incompetent; only a judge can restore her ability to make her own healthcare decisions."
"Competency is determined by the treating physician, whereas capacity is a broader legal category decided by a judge."

"Capacity for a specific healthcare decision is determined by a physician, while competency is determined by a judge and refers to more global decision-making; her psychosis does not automatically preclude capacity."
"Capacity and competency are interchangeable terms, so either the team or a judge may determine them for this specific decision."
"A patient with active psychosis is presumed incompetent for all healthcare decisions until she is treated and returns to her baseline."

explanation_correct: Capacity is determined by a physician for a specific healthcare-related decision (eg, to refuse medical care), whereas competency is determined by a judge and usually refers to more global categories of decision-making (eg, legally unable to make any healthcare-related decision). Additionally, mental illness is not an exclusion criterion unless the condition presently impairs the patient's ability to make the specific decision. The intern conflated the two concepts and overgeneralized from the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Incompetence is not automatically established by psychosis, and a judge does not 'restore' ability; the physician must first assess capacity for the specific decision.
explanation_incorrect.B: This reverses the two concepts: capacity is the physician's determination for a specific decision, and competency is the judge's more global legal determination.
explanation_incorrect.D: Capacity and competency are distinct — one clinical and decision-specific, the other legal and global — and cannot be used interchangeably.
explanation_incorrect.E: Active psychosis does not create a global presumption of incompetency; the patient's present ability to make the specific decision must be assessed.

educationalObjective: Capacity is a physician's determination for a specific decision; competency is a judge's broader legal determination, and psychiatric diagnosis alone does not negate capacity.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 45-year-old man with acute psychosis from his first manic episode insists that his severe right lower-quadrant pain is caused by "demons" and believes the hospital staff are poisoning his food. Imaging shows acute appendicitis with early signs of perforation. When asked, he cannot explain what appendicitis means or why the surgeons are recommending an operation, and he refuses surgery on the grounds that he does not trust "the poisoned hospital."
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?

options.text: Immediately take him to the operating room without further discussion, because his refusal is automatically invalid in a life-threatening illness.
Obtain a court order declaring him incompetent before proceeding with any treatment.
Accept his refusal as final, because a psychiatric illness can never be used to override a patient's stated wishes.
Ask his wife to sign the consent form but postpone surgery until his psychosis fully resolves.
Determine that he presently lacks capacity to refuse surgery for this decision, and obtain consent from his legal surrogate — or proceed under implied consent if surgery cannot wait.

explanation_correct: The physician must determine whether the patient is psychologically and legally capable of making this particular decision. This patient cannot appreciate what his condition means or why the operation is recommended, so his condition presently impairs his decision-making and he lacks capacity for this refusal. When a patient lacks decision-making capacity, consent should be obtained from a legal surrogate; if an emergency does not allow time, implied consent may apply. Psychiatric illness is not an automatic exclusion criterion, but here it is presently impairing.

explanation_incorrect.A: Even when a refusal is invalid, the physician should document that the patient lacks capacity for this specific decision and pursue surrogate or implied consent rather than operating without any assessment.
explanation_incorrect.B: Judicial declaration of competency is unnecessary and too slow; capacity for this specific decision is determined by the treating physician.
explanation_incorrect.C: Although mental illness is not an automatic bar, it can preclude capacity when it presently impairs the patient's ability to make the healthcare decision, as it does here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Delaying surgery for a progressing appendicitis until psychiatric symptoms resolve could allow perforation; surrogate consent for the urgent operation is the appropriate route.

educationalObjective: A patient lacks decision-making capacity when present impairment prevents appreciation of the condition and treatment; surrogate or implied consent then governs.
